raw_case_text:
The patient was a 56-year-old Ethiopian immigrant who moved to Italy in 1974. Symptoms started 17 days after returning from a 6-week holiday trip to Cote d'Ivoire (June 28-August 8, 2004). The patient had stayed both in rural and urban areas. She had not taken any malaria chemoprophylaxis during the trip. Three days after onset of fever with recurrent vomiting episodes she referred to the family doctor and she was treated with antibiotic; malaria was not clinically suspected. On arrival on August 25, the patient was dehydrated and pyrexial with a temperature of 37.8 C. Initial laboratory studies showed high creatinine level (2.42 mg/dL; reference range 0.50-1.10), uremia (urea 192 mg/dL; reference range 18-48), hyperglycaemia (glucose 794 mg/dL; reference range 70-110), lactic acidosis (lactic acid 3.1 mmoli/L; reference range 0.60-1.80), hypocalcemia (calcium 6.56 mg/dL; reference range 8.50-10.50), hyponatraemia (sodium 129 mmoli/L; reference range 132-143), anaemia (haemoglobin 7.9 g/dL; reference range 12.0-16.0), thrombocytopenia (platelet count 6 x 109/L; low-normal 140 x 109/L), and high levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) (CRP 13.4 mg/dL; reference range = 0.0-0.5 mg/dL). The results of the rest of the routine blood tests were within normal limits. A blood smear detected a P. falciparum, with a density of 40% of parasitized red blood cells (RBCs). A chest X-ray performed showed right middle lobe pneumonia and moderate bilateral pleural effusion. The patient was screened for Human immunodeficiency virus, Parvovirus B19, Hepatitis B virus, Hepatitis C virus, Coxsackie B 1-6, Cytomegalovirus; Herpes Simplex Virus 1 and 2, Epstein-Barr virus, and enteric fever. The patient was admitted to intensive care unit (ICU) and she was treated for 7 days with intravenous quinine 10 mg/kg every 8 hours after an initial loading dose of 20 mg/kg, for 7 days with doxycycline 100 mg.iv. every 12 hours and for 14 days with ceftriaxone 2 gr once a day. Hyperglycemia was controlled by applying an intensive insulin protocol with a target glycemia of 150 mg/dL. During the acute phase the patient was described with angina pectoris with normal troponin T levels; ECG showed T-wave alterations and echocardiography a global left ventricular hypokinesia; a supportive care with dopamine and nitrates was necessary. On followup, ECG and echocardiography had normalized. From August 25 to August 29, 2004 she was transfused with 6 units of compatible packed red cells (PRC), 3 unit random platelet concentrates (RPCs), and 4 units of fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) obtained by apheresis.
24 hours after starting quinine the parasitemia decreased by 50% and less insulin was needed to achieve glucose control. Thick and thin smears obtained 72 hours after therapy were negative for parasites. 
The insulin was injected subcutaneously according to blood glucose control since September 2. She did not need insulin since September 3. Her fasting blood sugar was in the normal range when discharged on September 9, 2004.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old female presenting with high fever, intractable vomiting, severe dehydration, and extreme lethargy 17 days after returning from Cote d'Ivoire.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 17 days after returning from a 6-week trip to Cote d'Ivoire with fever and recurrent vomiting. Three days into the illness, an outpatient physician prescribed oral antibiotics without improvement. Upon hospital arrival, she was markedly dehydrated, pyrexial, and in hyperosmolar state with acute renal failure and severe bicytopenia. During intensive care admission, she developed acute angina pectoris with ischemic ECG changes and transient myocardial hypokinesia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immigrated to Italy from Ethiopia in 1974. Traveled to Cote d'Ivoire for 6 weeks (staying in both rural and urban areas) without chemoprophylaxis. No prior history of diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, recurrent vomiting, dehydration, polyuria, chest tightness (angina), and weakness. Medications: oral antibiotics prescribed 3 days prior. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 37.8 C, marked dehydration. Cardiovascular: Tachycardia, angina pectoris noted during acute illness. Respiratory: Decreased breath sounds at bilateral bases and right middle lung zone. Abdominal and neurological exams were otherwise non-focal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 7.9 g/dL (reference: 12.0-16.0 g/dL), platelet count: 6 x 10^9/L (low-normal: 140 x 10^9/L). Serum creatinine: 2.42 mg/dL (reference: 0.50-1.10 mg/dL), serum urea: 192 mg/dL (reference: 18-48 mg/dL), blood glucose: 794 mg/dL (reference: 70-110 mg/dL), serum lactic acid: 3.1 mmol/L (reference: 0.60-1.80 mmol/L), serum calcium: 6.56 mg/dL (reference: 8.50-10.50 mg/dL), serum sodium: 129 mmol/L (reference: 132-143 mmol/L), C-reactive protein (CRP): 13.4 mg/dL (reference: 0.0-0.5 mg/dL). Cardiac troponin T: Normal. Chest radiograph: Right middle lobe pneumonia and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. 12-lead ECG: Diffuse T-wave alterations (normalized on follow-up). Transthoracic echocardiogram: Global left ventricular hypokinesia (normalized on follow-up). Screening serologies: HIV, Parvovirus B19, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, Coxsackie B1-6, CMV, HSV-1/2, EBV, and enteric fever tests all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hyperparasitemic severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (40% parasitemia) complicated by severe lactic acidosis, profound thrombocytopenia (6 x 10^9/L), acute kidney injury, new-onset severe stress hyperglycemia / diabetic ketoacidosis-like state, right middle lobe pneumonia, and transient stress cardiomyopathy (angina with global LV hypokinesia).
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitemia density of 40% parasitized red blood cells. Parasitemia decreased by 50% within 24 hours of quinine therapy and cleared completely by 72 hours (thick and thin films negative). Multiple acute viral and enteric pathogens were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to ICU. Treated with intravenous quinine (20 mg/kg loading dose, then 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days), intravenous doxycycline (100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days), and intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g once daily for 14 days). Resuscitation included transfusions of 6 units of packed red cells, 3 units of platelet concentrates, and 4 units of fresh frozen plasma. Glycemia was controlled using an intensive intravenous insulin protocol; insulin was discontinued on September 3 with normal fasting glucose. Cardiac ischemia/dysfunction was treated with dopamine and nitroglycerin with complete echocardiographic and ECG normalization. The patient made a full recovery and was discharged on September 9, 2004.
